Preflight Assessment
Preflight Checklist
Basics
Ensures the airplane meets airworthiness standards and is in a safe condition prior to flight
The preflight logically moves around the airplane to ensure it is in a condition for safe flight
Begins while approaching the airplane on the ramp – Note the overall appearance / any issues
The POH must be the reference for the preflight inspection (Chapter 4)
Always have a checklist on hand as a reference to ensure everything is checked
CE: Failure to use, or the improper use, of a checklist
CE: Hazards which may result from distractions interrupting an inspection
What to Inspect 									AI.V.A.K3a, AI.V.A.K3b
Inside the Flight deck
Airworthiness - Required Documents (AROW)
Logbooks – Ensure tests/inspections complied with (may not be kept in the plane) AI.V.A.K3d
Preflight Checklist items
Items located inside the airplane & items controlled inside the plane (lights, pitot heat, etc.)
Exterior of the Airplane
Follow the checklist and inspect all exterior portions of the airplane
CE: Inability to recognize discrepancies to determine airworthiness
Detecting Problems 										AI.V.A.K3c
Visible Structural Damage (follow the POH procedures and inspection requirements)
Check for dents, cracks, bending, separating, etc.
Check for leaks/stains as they are signs of potential problems
Look for missing rivets, bolts, etc.
Inspect the propeller for damage including nicks and cracking
Flight Controls
Move freely/correctly and are properly attached
Check the flap movement and connections
Fuel Quantity & Contamination
Confirm the fuel quantity indicated on the gauge
Contamination
Type, Grade of Fuel – Critical to safe flight (100LL (AVGAS) – Blue with a familiar gasoline scent)
80 is Red; 100LL is Blue; 100 is Green; Jet Fuel is Clear (kerosene scent)
Water and Other Sediment
Water is heavier than fuel and therefore accumulates in the low points
Sediment can come from dust/dirt entering the tanks
Check the grade and remove water and other contamination
Oil Quantity & Contamination
Verify the oil is at an acceptable amount
Check the oil when the engine is cold (proper reading, oil is settled at the bottom)
Contamination can be detected by discoloration
Oil darkens as operating hours increase; rapidly dark oil may point to cylinder problems
Leaks (Fuel, Oil, Hydraulic)
Verify no leaks under the plane, in the cowling, on the struts, etc.
CE: Failure to ensure servicing with the proper fuel and oil
Ice & Frost
Small amounts of ice/frost can disrupt the airflow over the wing, increase stall speed, and reduce lift
Do not fly unless the ice/frost is removed in accordance with the requirements in the POH
Loading & Securing
Ensure everything is properly loaded and secured prior to flight (verify the CG matches)
Secure everything properly to prevent movement during flight (possible damage or CG change)
CE: Failure to ensure proper loading/securing of baggage, cargo, and equipment
Determining the Airplane is Safe 								AI.V.A.K2
During the preflight, note any issues and make an educated go/no go decision
If there are questions as to whether the airplane is safe, ask for help (CFI, maintenance, etc.)
Follow the recommendations in the POH, as well as those learned from experience
Do not let emotion, outside pressure, or any undue influence sway you from safety
For inoperative equipment, follow the procedures in III.B. Airworthiness Requirements and 91.213(d)
Remember, FAR 91.3: The PIC is the final authority to the operation of the aircraft
Conclusion: Brief review of the main points

paragraphs.text: V.B. Flight Deck Management
Introduction
How
Occupant Briefing (SAFETY)									AI.V.B.K1
Seat Belts, Should harnesses, Seat positioned & locked
FAR 91.107 – Must brief passengers on how to fasten & unfasten their safety belt/shoulder harness
Seat belts required for taxi, takeoff, and landing; Shoulder harness required for takeoff and landing
Air vents, All environmental controls, Action in case of discomfort
Fire extinguisher location & operation
Exit doors operation, Emergency evacuation plan, Emergency/survival kit location & contents
Traffic (scanning, spotting, notifying pilot), Talking (sterile flick deck expectations)
Your Questions?
For more details, see the FAASafety Passenger Briefing Card
Arranging & Securing 									AI.V.B.K4
Arranging
Ensure that all the necessary equipment, documents, checklists, and charts are on board
Materials should be organized in a manner that makes them readily available for use
Securing
Check for loose items which might be tossed about during flight, or if turbulence is encountered
Form the habit of “good housekeeping;” in the long run, it will pay off in safer and more efficient flying
CE: Failure to place/secure essential materials and equipment for easy access during flight
Seat Position & Controls
Seat Belt/Harnesses
When seated, the seat belt/harness should be adjusted to a comfortable, snug fit
Shoulder harness must be worn at least for taxi, takeoff, and landing
The safety belt must be worn all times at the controls
Seats
On each flight, the pilot should be seated in the same position. Verify the seat is locked in position
Rudder Pedals
Adjust the rudder pedals forward or backward ensuring full/comfortable range of motion
Common Errors
Failure to properly adjust flight deck items, like safety belts, harnesses, rudder pedals, seat
Failure to provide proper adjustment of equipment and controls
Navigation Data Currency 									AI.V.B.K3
Charts
FAR 91.103 requires each PIC to become familiar with all available information concerning that flight
Although it doesn’t specifically require it, you should always carry current charts
Information changes rapidly, out of date charts may be missing crucial information
To confirm currency, refer to the next scheduled edition date printed on the cover
Use Dates of Latest Editions & check NOTAMs and Safety Alerts and Charting Notices for changes
Database Currency
AIM 1-1-17b1(c)(2) Database Currency: Databases must be updated for IFR operations
Databases should be updated for all other operations
No such requirement for databases to up updated for VFR navigation, however it is always a good idea
Violations
It is not FAA policy to initiate enforcement action against a pilot for having an old chart or no chart, or for having an expired navigation database

However, if a pilot is involved in an investigation and there’s evidence an out-of-date chart/database (or no chart) contributed to the situation, that information could be used in any enforcement action
Checklist Usage 										AI.V.B.K2
Ensure the proper and orderly use of the manufacturer’s checklist
Ensures every item is completed and checked in a logical order
Don’t go on memory, always backup your actions with a checklist
RM: Inoperative Equipment 									AI.V.B.R2
On the Ground
Perform a thorough preflight
Follow FAR 91.213(d) procedures to defer & placard equipment as inoperative
See III.B. Airworthiness Requirements
Consider the effects the inoperative equipment will have on the flight
Set and follow personal equipment minimums – just because it’s legal, doesn’t mean it’s safe
Airborne
If equipment becomes inoperative, a decision must be made to continue or divert
Considerations
Would the equipment prevent flying if it happened on the ground? FAR 91.213(d)
How does it affect the remainder of the flight or personal minimums?
Other thoughts based on the situation
Resource Utilization
Resources can be found both inside and outside the flight deck. Think outside the box if necessary
Internal Resources
POH, checklists (normal and emergency), charts
Satellite and/or app data, if equipped; documents loaded on a tablet
Equipment - A thorough understanding of the equipment is necessary to fully utilize all resources
Passengers can look for traffic, provide helpful information
Ingenuity, knowledge, and skill
External Resources
Maintenance technicians, and flight service personnel, 1800 WX Brief
Internet research (before flight – weather, NOTAMs, TFRs, airport procedures, etc.)
ATC – traffic advisories, vectors, emergency assistance, may even be able to contact someone
FSS can provide weather, airport conditions
Other airplanes can provide PIREPs as well as radio communications
ASOS/AWOS can also provide weather conditions in flight
CE: Failure to utilize all resources required to operate a flight safely
RM: Aviate, Navigate, Communicate
Distractions
RM: Passengers Distractions 								AI.V.B.R3
Use the preflight briefing as an opportunity to explain passenger expectations, sterile cockpit, etc.
If a passenger is distracting, explain the situation to them, and ask them to stop
Other Distractions: They’re dangerous, remove them from your view
RM: Automation & PEDs (RM: Use of systems or equipment, including automation & PEDs) 	AI.V.B.R1
Ensure understanding of equipment, systems, automation, electronic devices
Great tools for SA & reduced workload, but a lack of understanding can quickly distract from flying
Over reliance on automation/technology creates an environment where basic airmanship is eroded
Understand their operation, use them, but be able to fly proficiently/safely without them
Case Study: Eastern 401
Multi-pilot airplanes have crashed due to minor distractions
Eastern 401 crashed while preoccupied with a bulb and the pilots didn’t realize the autopilot turned off
Resources
YouTube Video (3 mins)
FAA Lessons Learned: Accident Board Findings & Key Safety Issues
Risk Management Concepts
Excess of technology, loss of SA, distractions, systems understanding & malfunctions, task prioritization
Discuss ways to mitigate these risks
Extremely important in a single pilot aircraft that you divide attention, avoid distraction & maintain SA
Conclusion: Brief review of the main points

Adjust the rudder pedals forward or backward ensuring full/comfortable range of motion
Common Errors
Failure to properly adjust flight deck items, like safety belts, harnesses, rudder pedals, seat
Failure to provide proper adjustment of equipment and controls
Navigation Data Currency 									AI.V.B.K3
Charts
FAR 91.103 requires each PIC to become familiar with all available information concerning that flight
Although it doesn’t specifically require it, you should always carry current charts
Information changes rapidly, out of date charts may be missing crucial information
To confirm currency, refer to the next scheduled edition date printed on the cover
Use Dates of Latest Editions & check NOTAMs and Safety Alerts and Charting Notices for changes
Database Currency
AIM 1-1-17b1(c)(2) Database Currency: Databases must be updated for IFR operations
Databases should be updated for all other operations
No such requirement for databases to up updated for VFR navigation, however it is always a good idea
Violations
It is not FAA policy to initiate enforcement action against a pilot for having an old chart or no chart, or for having an expired navigation database
However, if a pilot is involved in an investigation and there’s evidence an out-of-date chart/database (or no chart) contributed to the situation, that information could be used in any enforcement action
Checklist Usage 										AI.V.B.K2
Ensure the proper and orderly use of the manufacturer’s checklist
Ensures every item is completed and checked in a logical order
Don’t go on memory, always backup your actions with a checklist
RM: Inoperative Equipment 									AI.V.B.R2
On the Ground
Perform a thorough preflight
Follow FAR 91.213(d) procedures to defer & placard equipment as inoperative
See III.B. Airworthiness Requirements
Consider the effects the inoperative equipment will have on the flight
Set and follow personal equipment minimums – just because it’s legal, doesn’t mean it’s safe
Airborne
If equipment becomes inoperative, a decision must be made to continue or divert
Considerations
Would the equipment prevent flying if it happened on the ground? FAR 91.213(d)
How does it affect the remainder of the flight or personal minimums?
Other thoughts based on the situation
Resource Utilization
Resources can be found both inside and outside the flight deck. Think outside the box if necessary
Internal Resources
POH, checklists (normal and emergency), charts
Satellite and/or app data, if equipped; documents loaded on a tablet
Equipment - A thorough understanding of the equipment is necessary to fully utilize all resources
Passengers can look for traffic, provide helpful information
Ingenuity, knowledge, and skill
External Resources
Maintenance technicians, and flight service personnel, 1800 WX Brief
Internet research (before flight – weather, NOTAMs, TFRs, airport procedures, etc.)
ATC – traffic advisories, vectors, emergency assistance, may even be able to contact someone
FSS can provide weather, airport conditions
Other airplanes can provide PIREPs as well as radio communications
ASOS/AWOS can also provide weather conditions in flight
CE: Failure to utilize all resources required to operate a flight safely
RM: Aviate, Navigate, Communicate
Distractions
RM: Passengers Distractions 								AI.V.B.R3
Use the preflight briefing as an opportunity to explain passenger expectations, sterile cockpit, etc.
If a passenger is distracting, explain the situation to them, and ask them to stop
Other Distractions: They’re dangerous, remove them from your view
RM: Automation & PEDs (RM: Use of systems or equipment, including automation & PEDs) 	AI.V.B.R1
Ensure understanding of equipment, systems, automation, electronic devices
Great tools for SA & reduced workload, but a lack of understanding can quickly distract from flying
Over reliance on automation/technology creates an environment where basic airmanship is eroded
Understand their operation, use them, but be able to fly proficiently/safely without them
Case Study: Eastern 401
Multi-pilot airplanes have crashed due to minor distractions
Eastern 401 crashed while preoccupied with a bulb and the pilots didn’t realize the autopilot turned off
Resources
YouTube Video (3 mins)
FAA Lessons Learned: Accident Board Findings & Key Safety Issues
Risk Management Concepts
Excess of technology, loss of SA, distractions, systems understanding & malfunctions, task prioritization
Discuss ways to mitigate these risks
Extremely important in a single pilot aircraft that you divide attention, avoid distraction & maintain SA
Conclusion: Brief review of the main points

paragraphs.text: V.C. Engine Starting
Introduction
How
POH
Checklists
Always use Manufacturer Checklists
Ensures every item is completed and checked in a logical order
RM: Engine Starting Limitations 							AI.V.C.K3, AI.V.C.R3
Review associated engine start limitations in the POH
RM: Safety Precautions (RM: Propeller Safety) 						AI.V.C.R1
Before Start
Set the parking brake and/or hold the toe brakes (look outside to verify you’re not moving)
Ensure the ramp area surrounding the airplane is clear of persons, equipment, and other hazards
Be aware of what is in front of, to the side, and behind the airplane
Anti-collision lights should be turned on prior to any start, at night use position lights too
Always call “CLEAR” out of the side window and wait for a response
When activating the starter, the wheel brakes must be depressed and/or parking bake set (check POH)
Engine Controls During Start
Always keep one hand on the throttle
After the engine is started, set the throttle and other controls as specified in the POH
Monitor oil pressure after engine start
In most conditions, oil pressure should reach at least the lower limit within 30 seconds
If oil pressure does not rise to the POH values in the specified time, shutdown the engine
Avoid excessive engine RPM and temperatures
Monitor the instruments and use the checklist if engine temperature begins to rise abnormally
Common Errors
Improper adjustment of engine controls during start
Failure to use safety precautions related to starting, and ensure clearance of the prop
Engine Starting
Normal Start Checklist
Review the normal start checklist in the POH
Atmospheric Conditions 									AI.V.C.K1
Cold Weather
Cold Engine Start Problems
Less effective batteries, and stuck instruments
Congealed Oil: Makes the prop more difficult to move (both with the starter and by hand)
Tendency to Over Prime: Washes down cylinder walls and may result in scoring of the walls
Results in poor compression/hard starting; fires have been started by over priming
Iced Sparkplugs: Engine fires a few revolutions and then quits. The only remedy is heat
Preheat of the engine(s) (and cabin) before start is desirable (hangar, cowl heaters, etc.)
Starting Procedure
Follow the POH procedures for a cold start (review POH procedures/checklists)
Prime the engine with fuel first (over-priming can result in fire – AC 91-13. Cancelled but useful)
After start, follow the POH procedures to allow the engine and oil to warm and circulate
Hot Weather
Unless very hot, normal start procedures will generally work (use hot start procedures, if needed)
Generally, little to no priming is needed. If the engine doesn’t catch, use minimal priming
In the case of an over primed engine, follow the flooded start checklist
Vapor lock (fuel injected engines)
Fuel delivery lines tend to be on the top of the engine, directly over the cylinder fins
Engine + outside heat can boil the fuel out of the lines creating vapor which can prevent starting
Hot start procedures should be used to purge the lines of vapor
Review Hot Weather Engine Starting checklist(s) and procedures
External Power Start		 							AI.V.C.K2, AI.V.C.R2
Provides another source of power if the battery is dead
RM: Ensure proper use and understanding of the external power unit
Follow steps in the owner’s manual
Besides not being able to start the plane, there is the risk of damaging the unit or aircraft systems
Follow the procedures prescribed in the POH
Be extremely cautious of people and equipment near the propeller during engine start (have a plan)
RM: Hand Propping Safety (RM: Propeller Safety) 						AI.V.C.R1
Basic requirements BEFORE attempting a hand prop
Do not hand prop unless two people, both familiar with hand propping techniques are available
The person pulling the propeller blades through directs all activity and is in charge of the procedure
The 2nd person is in the plane with brakes set, operating the controls, and following instructions
The ground surface near the prop should be stable and free of debris
Both participants should discuss the procedure and agree on voice commands and expected action
Engine Starting Set-up
Unless otherwise specified, the descending prop blade should be slightly above horizontal
Person doing the propping should face the blade squarely and stand less than an arm’s length away
Too far away results in leaning forward into the prop in an unbalanced condition
Procedures and Commands for Hand Propping
Follow the procedures specified in the POH. Have a plan
Common Errors
Failure to use safety precautions related to starting
Failure to ensure proper clearance of the propeller
Conclusion:
Brief review of the main points

paragraphs.text: V.D. Taxiing, Airport Signs, & Lighting
Introduction
How
Taxi Instructions 										AI.V.D.K3
Controlled Airports (AIM 4-3-18 Taxiing) 							AI.V.D.K7b
Communicating with ATC (Big Picture)
Always use standard ATC phraseology to facilitate clear and concise communication
When making initial contact, state who you are, where you are on the airport, what you want
Focus on the ATC clearance
Don’t perform any nonessential tasks while communicating with ATC
Read back all clearances and verify the route/clearance on the taxi diagram
RM: Eliminate expectation bias 							AI.V.D.R2
Clearance is Required:
To taxi onto the movement area
To taxi on a runway, take off, or land when an ATC tower is in operation
Prior to crossing any runway (ATC will issue an explicit clearance for all runway crossings)
Contact Ground
Prior to entering the movement area, contact Ground control for taxi clearance
Ground Frequencies & Procedures
Reference the Chart Supplement, Airport Diagram, check NOTAMs for changes, closures, etc.
Taxi Request
Aircraft identification, location, type of operation (VFR/IFR), first point of intended landing
When assigned a takeoff runway, ground will:
Specify the runway (or point to taxi to)
Issue taxi instructions
State any hold short instructions or runway crossing clearances
After taxi instructions are received, always read back:
Runway assignment
Any clearance to enter a specific runway
Any instruction to hold short of a specific runway or line up and wait
Controllers are required to request readback of hold short instructions if not received
Uncontrolled Airports 									AI.V.D.K7b
Planning
Be familiar with the local procedures, runway use, traffic pattern direction and altitude
Be alert, communicate intentions on the CTAF and listen for other aircraft
Communication
Monitor/communicate on the CTAF from engine start, taxi, and until 10 miles from the airport
Announce location and intentions on the CTAF
Maintain Situational Awareness
Plan, Brief, Review 										AI.V.D.K7a
Route Planning
Review the Chart Supplement & airport diagram (ensure current charts/pubs)		AI.V.D.K2
Review any pre-designated, or standard, taxi routes
Review NOTAMs, expected route(s), hot spots, etc.
Using this information, build a general idea of the airport layout and a likely route
Taxi Brief
Passenger Info (can start here, if the passenger brief isn’t already completed)
SAFETY brief (FAASafety Passenger Briefing Card)
Described in V.B. Flight Deck Management
Technical Info
Verify fuel plan & load (required fuel versus what is onboard)
Equipment issues (are any systems/equipment inoperative and how it affects the flight)
NOTAMs affecting the taxi route (taxiway/runway closures, constructions, etc.)
Expected departure runway, route, and overall plan (may change based on ATC instruction)
Critical locations (abnormalities, hot spots, taxiway/runway closures, NOTAMs, etc.)
Any other pertinent information
Record & Review
Request & obtain taxi clearance
Always write down ATC taxi instructions to prevent mistakes
Review the route given by ATC, ask for help in case of confusion
Benefits
Prevents mistakes and forgetfulness
RM: Combats expectation bias 							AI.V.D.R2
Increases SA
Clear up confusions/questions prior to moving
Operate with your head up/eyes outside to the max extent
Taxiing
RM: Appropriate Flight Deck Activities (RM: Activities & Distractions) 		AI.V.D.K7a, AI.V.D.R1
For safety reasons the pilot’s workload should be at a minimum during taxi operations
Complete pre-taxi checklists and data entry prior to taxi
All heads down activities should be accomplished when the aircraft is stopped
A sterile flight deck should be implemented from taxi through climb to focus on taxiing/ATC
Remove distractions from view (if a person, explain the situation and ask them to stop)
Taxiing Near Other Aircraft
Use a “continuous loop” process to monitor & update their progress and location in relation to you
Awareness is enhanced by understanding the clearance issued to other pilots/aircraft and vehicles
Basics
Steering: Accomplished with the rudder pedals and brakes
To turn, apply rudder in the desired direction; inside brake can also be applied to tighten the turn
Rudder should be held until just short of the point where the turn is to be stopped
Pressure is then released, or opposite pressure is applied to maintain centerline
Brakes: Used to stop, slow, or aid in making a turn and should be applied smoothly and evenly
Speed: Taxi at the speed of a fast walk
Controlled 1st with power and 2nd with brake pressure - Don’t ride the brakes
Centerline: Describe site picture for specific aircraft
Stopping: Ensure the nose wheel straight to prevent side loading and to make moving again easier
Common Errors
Hazards of taxiing too fast
Improper use of brakes
Taxi Checks
Brakes: Test the brakes for proper operation as soon as the airplane is put in motion
Attitude Indicator: No more than 5o of pitch or bank indicated
Turn & Slip Indicator: Wings move with the turn/Ball opposite the turn/Inclinometer is full of fluid
Compass & Heading Indicator: Moving toward known headings (no cracks, leaks, bubbles)
Aircraft Lighting										AI.V.D.K6
Engines Running: Rotating beacon on
Taxiing: Prior to moving, turn on navigation, position, and anti-collision lights
Turn on the taxi light when moving or intending to move - turn it off when stopped or yielding
Strobe lights should not be used during taxi if they adversely affect the vision of others
Crossing a Runway: All exterior lights should be illuminated when crossing a runway
Entering the Runway: Turn on all lights, except for landing lights
Takeoff: Landing lights on when takeoff clearance is received or when commencing takeoff roll
Wind Corrections 										AI.V.D.K5
Recognizing Wind Direction
ATIS, ATC, FSS can provide wind direction
Wind Indicators
Windsock or Cone: Wind direction is opposite the direction the sock is pointing
Tetrahedron & Wind Tee: Move freely and align with the wind direction
Generally, located in a central location near the runway
Use the heading indicator/heading bug to visualize wind in relation to the airplane
Control Applications
Quartering Headwind: Ailerons turned into the wind and the elevator is held neutral
Quartering Tailwind: Controls are positioned to dive with the wind (tailwind requires less power)
Night Operations 										AI.V.D.K7d
Exterior lights make an aircraft on the airport surface easier to see 			AI.V.D.K6
On the Runway: Line up slightly (3’) off the centerline to differentiate you from the runway lights
Be more cautious at night
Reduced visibility makes taxiing more difficult
Taxi slower
Low Visibility (AIM 4-3-19) 									AI.V.D.K7e
Focus entire attention on the safe operation of the aircraft while it is moving
Taxi slowly with focus outside
Sterile flight deck
Withold checklists and nonessential communication until stopped with the brakes set
Notify the controller of difficulties or at the first indication of becoming disoriented
RM: Runway Incursions 									AI.V.D.R4
Taxi First: Sterile flight deck, eyes outside, stop in the case of an emergency
If a checklist needs to be completed, or attention needs to be diverted from taxiing, wait until stopped
In the case of an emergency, stop the aircraft immediately and proceed as required
Maintain Situational Awareness
Know where you are and where you’re going – have a taxi diagram
Build a mental picture of other traffic on the airport
Communication Matters
Write down complex instructions, especially at unfamiliar airports
Read back all runway/taxiway crossing and hold instructions using proper phraseology/good discipline
Be Conservative
Taxi at a safe speed (fast walk)
RM: Route and/or Runway Change 								AI.V.D.R3
Ask for a safe place to stop, if necessary
Copy the new taxi instructions and review the route
Request progressive, if necessary
Entering/Crossing Runways 									AI.V.D.K7c
A specific clearance is required to cross all runways
Hold Lines
Approaching from the dashed side, cross (no clearance required) & stop fully passed the solid lines
Approaching from the solid side, do not cross without clearance
Prior to crossing hold lines, clear both directions (approach path & runway surface)
Lights on, as discussed
Landing and Rollout
Brief the landing/rollout plan
After landing, ensure that the entire aircraft has crossed the landing runway’s hold short line
If stopped between parallel runways, only cross when cleared to cross
Airport Markings 										AI.V.D.K4
Runway Markings
Three Types of Runway Markings (see diagram, below)
Visual; Nonprecision Instrument; Precision Instrument
Diagram Notes
Note 1: Required on runways serving category C & D aircraft, and for runways intended for international commercial air transport
Note 2: Required on 4,200’ or longer runways serving categories C & D airplanes
Note 3: Required on 4,200’ or longer instrumented runways
Note 4: Used when the full runway pavement width may not be available for use as a runway
Runway Designators
Purpose - To identify / differentiate runways from the approach end
Magnetic North; whole number to the nearest one-tenth of the runway course
L, R, C differentiate multiple parallel runways
Markings - Large white numbers
Runway Centerline Marking
Purpose - Identifies the center of the runway providing alignment guidance for takeoff and landing
Markings - A line of uniformly spaced stripes and gaps
Runway Aiming Point Markings
Purpose - Visual aiming point for landing
Markings - Broad white stripe on each side of the centerline, approximately 1,000’ from threshold
Runway Touchdown Zone Markers
Purpose - Identifies touchdown zone for landing; provide distance info in 500’ increments
Markings - Groups of 1, 2, and 3 rectangular bars in pairs about the runway centerline
Runway Side Stripe Markings
Purpose - Delineate edges of the runway providing a contrast between the runway and shoulder
Markings - Continuous white stripes located on each side of the runway
Runway Shoulder Markings
Purpose - Identify pavement areas not intended for aircraft use
Markings - Yellow stripes
Runway Threshold Markings (stripes vary with width, chart to right)
Purpose - Identifies beginning of the runway available for landing
Markings - Stripes about the centerline
Displaced Threshold (DT)
Explanation
Landing threshold starts at a point other than the beginning of the runway
Used for taxiing, takeoff, landing rollout (not to be landed on, reduces landing distance)
Markings
A 10’ wide white threshold bar across the runway at the displaced threshold
White arrow heads are located across the runway just prior to the threshold bar
White arrows down the centerline between the start of the runway and displaced threshold
Relocated Threshold
Explanation – Construction / other activities require the threshold to be relocated (NOTAM)
Markings – Normally a 10’ wide white threshold bar across the runway, but can vary
Blast Pad / Stopway Area
Blast Pad: Area where a propeller or jet blast can dissipate without creating a hazard
Stopway: Space to decelerate / stop in the event of an aborted takeoff (chevrons)
Taxiway Markings
General
Taxiways should have centerline/runway holding position markings whenever intersecting a runway
Edge markings separate the taxiway from areas not for aircraft use or define taxiway edges
Taxiway Centerline Markings
Normal Centerline
Purpose - Provide a visual cue to permit taxiing along a designated path
Markings - A single continuous yellow line that is 6” - 12” wide
Enhanced Centerline
Purpose - Same as above but at larger commercial airports to warn that a runway hold position marking is being approached
Markings - Parallel line of yellow dashes on both sides of the taxiway centerline
Taxiway Edge Markings
Purpose - Defines the edge of the taxiway (usually when edge doesn’t match up with pavement)
Continuous Markings
Purpose - Define the taxiway edge from the shoulder/paved surface not for use by aircraft
Markings - Continuous double yellow line
Dashed Markings
Purpose - Define the taxiway edge when adjoining pavement is intended for aircraft (apron)
Markings - Broken double yellow line
Taxi Shoulder Markings

A circle with an outer black ring, inner white ring, and a pink circle

General

Purpose - Identify where to stop without a clearance onto the runway

Purpose - Only installed if normally used for LAHSO or taxiing ops

Purpose - Installed on taxiways where ATC normally holds aircraft short of an intersection

Purpose - Supplements signs located at the holding position

Purpose - Outline the edges of taxiways during periods of darkness or restricted visibility
Configuration - Blue light
Taxiway Centerline Lights
Purpose - Facilitate taxiing during low visibility conditions
Configuration - Steady green lights along the centerline
Clearance Bar Lights
Purpose - Installed to increase the visibility of a holding position in low visibility conditions
May also be installed to indicate the location of an intersecting taxiway during darkness
Configuration - Three in pavement steady yellow lights
Runway Guard Lights
Purpose - Enhance the visibility of taxiway and runway intersections
Configuration - Either a pair of elevated flashing yellow lights on either side of the taxiway, or a row of in pavement yellow lights across the entire taxiway at the runway hold marking
Stop Bar Lights
Purpose - Confirm ATC clearances to enter/cross an active runway in low visibility conditions
Configuration - Row of red, unidirectional, steady in pavement lights across the entire taxiway at the runway hold position, and elevated steady-burning red lights on either side
Following ATC clearance, the stop bar is turned off and the lead-on lights are turned on
Never cross a red illuminated stop bar even if you have received ATC clearance
If after crossing, the lead-on lights extinguish, hold position, and contact ATC for instruction

Installed to provide rapid / positive identification of the approach end of a runway
Configuration - Pair of synchronized flashing lights on each side of the runway threshold

Outline the edges of runways during dark / restricted visibility conditions
Classified according to intensity/brightness: High Intensity (HIRL); Medium (MIRL); Low (LIRL)
Configuration
Runway edge lights - White
Instrument runways – Yellow for the last 2,000,’ or half the runway, whichever is shorter
Lights marking the end of the runway – Red / Green
Red indicates the end of the runway to a departing aircraft
Green indicates the threshold to landing aircraft

Installed on some precision runways to facilitate landing under adverse conditions
Configuration
Along runway centerline at 50’ intervals
From the threshold, the lights are white until the last 3,000’ of the runway
White lights alternate with red for 2,000’, and the last 1,000’ all lights are red
Touchdown Zone Lights (TDZL)
On some precision runways to indicate touchdown zone in low visibility conditions
Configuration
Rows of (usually 3) lights on both sides of the runway centerline
Rows begin 100’ beyond the landing threshold and extend to 3,000’ beyond the landing threshold or the midpoint of the runway, whichever is less
Taxiway Centerline Lead-Off Lights
Provide visual guidance to exit the runway
Configuration
Alternate green & yellow lights, beginning with green, from the runway centerline to 1 light position beyond the runway hold position/ILS critical area hold position
Taxiway Centerline Lead-on Lights
Provide visual guidance for entering the runway
Configuration
Color coded with the same pattern as lead-off lights
Bidirectional (1 side emits light for the lead-on function the other for the lead-off)
Land and Hold Short Lights
Used to indicate the hold short point on certain runways approved for LAHSO
When installed, the lights will be on anytime LAHSO is in effect and off when not
Configuration - A row of pulsing white lights installed across the runway

Fully automated system indicating that it’s unsafe to enter, cross, takeoff, or land on a runway
Installed at several major US airports
Processes information from surveillance systems to turn red warning lights on/off
Used in conjunction with ATC – lights and ATC instructions must agree
Runway Entrance Lights (REL)
In-pavement red lights
Warns aircraft waiting to cross/enter a runway that there’s conflicting traffic
Takeoff Hold Lights (THL)
In-pavement red lights
Warns aircraft in the takeoff position that the runway is occupied & takeoff is unsafe
More details: FAA Runway Status Lights

Operation of approach light systems and runway lighting is controlled by the tower / FSS
Pilots may request the lights be turned on or off
Pilot Control of Airport Lighting
Radio control of lighting is available at some airports by keying the microphone
3 clicks for Low lights, 5 for Medium, and 7 for High
All clicks within 5 seconds – lasts 15 minutes
Frequency is in Chart Supplement/ instrument approach procedures publications (usually CTAF)

How
Taxi Instructions 										AI.V.D.K3
Controlled Airports (AIM 4-3-18 Taxiing) 							AI.V.D.K7b
Communicating with ATC (Big Picture)
Always use standard ATC phraseology to facilitate clear and concise communication
When making initial contact, state who you are, where you are on the airport, what you want
Focus on the ATC clearance
Don’t perform any nonessential tasks while communicating with ATC
Read back all clearances and verify the route/clearance on the taxi diagram
RM: Eliminate expectation bias 							AI.V.D.R2
Clearance is Required:
To taxi onto the movement area
To taxi on a runway, take off, or land when an ATC tower is in operation
Prior to crossing any runway (ATC will issue an explicit clearance for all runway crossings)
Contact Ground
Prior to entering the movement area, contact Ground control for taxi clearance
Ground Frequencies & Procedures
Reference the Chart Supplement, Airport Diagram, check NOTAMs for changes, closures, etc.
Taxi Request
Aircraft identification, location, type of operation (VFR/IFR), first point of intended landing
When assigned a takeoff runway, ground will:
Specify the runway (or point to taxi to)
Issue taxi instructions
State any hold short instructions or runway crossing clearances
After taxi instructions are received, always read back:
Runway assignment
Any clearance to enter a specific runway
Any instruction to hold short of a specific runway or line up and wait
Controllers are required to request readback of hold short instructions if not received
Uncontrolled Airports 									AI.V.D.K7b
Planning
Be familiar with the local procedures, runway use, traffic pattern direction and altitude
Be alert, communicate intentions on the CTAF and listen for other aircraft
Communication
Monitor/communicate on the CTAF from engine start, taxi, and until 10 miles from the airport
Announce location and intentions on the CTAF
Maintain Situational Awareness

Equipment issues (are any systems/equipment inoperative and how it affects the flight)

Expected departure runway, route, and overall plan (may change based on ATC instruction)
Critical locations (abnormalities, hot spots, taxiway/runway closures, NOTAMs, etc.)
Any other pertinent information

Basics
Steering: Accomplished with the rudder pedals and brakes
To turn, apply rudder in the desired direction; inside brake can also be applied to tighten the turn
Rudder should be held until just short of the point where the turn is to be stopped
Pressure is then released, or opposite pressure is applied to maintain centerline
Brakes: Used to stop, slow, or aid in making a turn and should be applied smoothly and evenly
Speed: Taxi at the speed of a fast walk
Controlled 1st with power and 2nd with brake pressure - Don’t ride the brakes
Centerline: Describe site picture for specific aircraft
Stopping: Ensure the nose wheel straight to prevent side loading and to make moving again easier
Common Errors
Hazards of taxiing too fast
Improper use of brakes

Brakes: Test the brakes for proper operation as soon as the airplane is put in motion
Attitude Indicator: No more than 5o of pitch or bank indicated

Taxiing: Prior to moving, turn on navigation, position, and anti-collision lights
Turn on the taxi light when moving or intending to move - turn it off when stopped or yielding

Use the heading indicator/heading bug to visualize wind in relation to the airplane
Control Applications
Quartering Headwind: Ailerons turned into the wind and the elevator is held neutral
Quartering Tailwind: Controls are positioned to dive with the wind (tailwind requires less power)

A specific clearance is required to cross all runways
Hold Lines
Approaching from the dashed side, cross (no clearance required) & stop fully passed the solid lines
Approaching from the solid side, do not cross without clearance
Prior to crossing hold lines, clear both directions (approach path & runway surface)
Lights on, as discussed

Brief the landing/rollout plan

Airport Markings 										AI.V.D.K4
Runway Markings
Three Types of Runway Markings (see diagram, below)
Visual; Nonprecision Instrument; Precision Instrument
Diagram Notes
Note 1: Required on runways serving category C & D aircraft, and for runways intended for international commercial air transport
Note 2: Required on 4,200’ or longer runways serving categories C & D airplanes
Note 3: Required on 4,200’ or longer instrumented runways
Note 4: Used when the full runway pavement width may not be available for use as a runway
Runway Designators
Purpose - To identify / differentiate runways from the approach end
Magnetic North; whole number to the nearest one-tenth of the runway course
L, R, C differentiate multiple parallel runways
Markings - Large white numbers
Runway Centerline Marking
Purpose - Identifies the center of the runway providing alignment guidance for takeoff and landing
Markings - A line of uniformly spaced stripes and gaps
Runway Aiming Point Markings
Purpose - Visual aiming point for landing
Markings - Broad white stripe on each side of the centerline, approximately 1,000’ from threshold
Runway Touchdown Zone Markers
Purpose - Identifies touchdown zone for landing; provide distance info in 500’ increments
Markings - Groups of 1, 2, and 3 rectangular bars in pairs about the runway centerline
Runway Side Stripe Markings
Purpose - Delineate edges of the runway providing a contrast between the runway and shoulder
Markings - Continuous white stripes located on each side of the runway
Runway Shoulder Markings
Purpose - Identify pavement areas not intended for aircraft use
Markings - Yellow stripes
Runway Threshold Markings (stripes vary with width, chart to right)
Purpose - Identifies beginning of the runway available for landing
Markings - Stripes about the centerline
Displaced Threshold (DT)
Explanation
Landing threshold starts at a point other than the beginning of the runway
Used for taxiing, takeoff, landing rollout (not to be landed on, reduces landing distance)
Markings
A 10’ wide white threshold bar across the runway at the displaced threshold
White arrow heads are located across the runway just prior to the threshold bar
White arrows down the centerline between the start of the runway and displaced threshold
Relocated Threshold
Explanation – Construction / other activities require the threshold to be relocated (NOTAM)
Markings – Normally a 10’ wide white threshold bar across the runway, but can vary
Blast Pad / Stopway Area
Blast Pad: Area where a propeller or jet blast can dissipate without creating a hazard
Stopway: Space to decelerate / stop in the event of an aborted takeoff (chevrons)
Taxiway Markings
General
Taxiways should have centerline/runway holding position markings whenever intersecting a runway
Edge markings separate the taxiway from areas not for aircraft use or define taxiway edges
Taxiway Centerline Markings
Normal Centerline
Purpose - Provide a visual cue to permit taxiing along a designated path
Markings - A single continuous yellow line that is 6” - 12” wide
Enhanced Centerline
Purpose - Same as above but at larger commercial airports to warn that a runway hold position marking is being approached
Markings - Parallel line of yellow dashes on both sides of the taxiway centerline
Taxiway Edge Markings
Purpose - Defines the edge of the taxiway (usually when edge doesn’t match up with pavement)
Continuous Markings
Purpose - Define the taxiway edge from the shoulder/paved surface not for use by aircraft
Markings - Continuous double yellow line
Dashed Markings
Purpose - Define the taxiway edge when adjoining pavement is intended for aircraft (apron)
Markings - Broken double yellow line
Taxi Shoulder Markings
Purpose - Prevent erosion but may not support aircraft
Markings - Taxiway edge markings will usually define this area
Surface Painted Taxiway Direction Signs
Purpose - When it isn’t possible to offer direction signs at intersections, or to supplement such signs
Markings - Surface painted location signs with a yellow background and black inscription
Surface Painted Location Signs
Purpose - Location signs assisting in confirming the taxiway
Markings - Black background with a yellow inscription
Geographic Position Markings
Purpose - Identifies aircraft location during low visibility operations
Markings - Left of the taxiway centerline in the direction of taxiing
A circle with an outer black ring, inner white ring, and a pink circle
On dark pavement the white/black ring are reversed
Holding Position Markings
General
Show where an aircraft is supposed to stop when approaching a runway (hold on the solid side)
4 yellow lines (2 solid/2 dashed) across the width of the taxiway/runway/approach area
Runway Holding Position Markings on Taxiways
Purpose - Identify where to stop without a clearance onto the runway
Runway Holding Position Markings on Runways (pictured, right)
Purpose - Only installed if normally used for LAHSO or taxiing ops
Must stop before markings/exit prior to reaching the position
Markings - White inscription/red background next to hold markings
Taxiways Located in Runway Approach Area
Holding Position Markings for Instrument Landing System (ILS)
Purpose - Hold aircraft when the ILS critical area is being protected
Markings - 2 yellow solid lines 2’ apart joined by pairs of solid lines 10’ apart across the taxiway
Holding Position Markings for Taxiways/Taxiway Intersections
Purpose - Installed on taxiways where ATC normally holds aircraft short of an intersection
Markings - Single dashed line extending across the width of the taxiway
Surface Painted Holding Position Signs (pictured, right)
Purpose - Supplements signs located at the holding position
Markings - Red background / white text, on hold side, before hold lines
Other Markings
Vehicle Roadway Markings
Purpose - Defines a path for vehicle operations on the airport
Markings - White solid line delineates each edge and a dashed line separates lanes
VOR Receiver Checkpoint Markings
Purpose - Allow the pilot to check aircraft instruments with navigational aid signals
Markings - Painted circle with an arrow in the middle (arrow is aligned toward the facility)
Located with a sign on the apron/taxiway – Black text on a yellow background
Nonmovement Area Boundary Markings (pictured, right)
Purpose - Delineates movement area (area under control)
Markings - 2 yellow lines (one solid and one dashed)
Marking & Lighting of Permanently Closed Runways
Purpose – Identify permanently closed runways/taxiways
Markings - The lighting circuits will be disconnected
Yellow crosses at each end of the runway and at 1,000’ intervals
Temporarily Closed Runways & Taxiways
Purpose – Indication that a runway is temporarily closed
Markings - Yellow crosses are placed on the runway at each end
A visual indication may not be present depending on the reason / duration of closure
Check NOTAMs / ATIS
Closed taxiways are blockaded (yellow cross may also be used)
Airport Signs 											AI.V.D.K4
Mandatory Instruction
Purpose - Denote entrance to runway or critical area / area where aircraft are prohibited
Markings - Red background with a white text
Typical Mandatory Signs and Applications
Runway Holding Position Sign
Runway Approach Area Holding Position Sign
ILS Critical Area Holding Position Sign
No Entry Sign
Location Signs
Purpose - Identify either a taxiway or runway on which the aircraft is located
Taxiway Location Sign
Purpose - Along taxiways to indicate location
Markings - Black background with yellow inscription and border
Runway Location Sign
Purpose - Complement compass/heading info; typically, in areas with multiple runways
Markings - Black background with yellow text
Runway Boundary Sign
Purpose - Visual cue depicting when “clear of the runway”
Markings - Yellow background / black lines
ILS Critical Area Boundary Sign
Purpose - Depicts where clear of the ILS critical area
Markings - Yellow background / black lines
Direction Signs
Purpose - Identify taxiways out of an intersection
Designations / arrows are arranged clockwise from the 1st taxiway on the pilot’s left
Markings - Yellow background / black text
Destination Signs
Purpose - Indicates a destination on the airport
Destinations commonly shown are
Markings – Yellow background/Black text
Information Signs
Purpose - Provide information on things such as:
Areas the tower can’t see, radio frequencies, and noise abatement procedures
Markings - Yellow Background / black text
Runway Distance Remaining Signs
Purpose – Informs the distance remaining on the runway
Number indicates the thousands of feet of landing runway remaining
Markings - Black background / white number
CE: Failure to comply with airport, runway, taxiway signs and markings
Airport Lighting & Visual Aids 								AI.V.D.K4
Taxiway Lighting
Taxiway Edge Lights
Purpose - Outline the edges of taxiways during periods of darkness or restricted visibility
Configuration - Blue light
Taxiway Centerline Lights
Purpose - Facilitate taxiing during low visibility conditions
Configuration - Steady green lights along the centerline
Clearance Bar Lights
Purpose - Installed to increase the visibility of a holding position in low visibility conditions
May also be installed to indicate the location of an intersecting taxiway during darkness
Configuration - Three in pavement steady yellow lights
Runway Guard Lights
Purpose - Enhance the visibility of taxiway and runway intersections
Configuration - Either a pair of elevated flashing yellow lights on either side of the taxiway, or a row of in pavement yellow lights across the entire taxiway at the runway hold marking
Stop Bar Lights
Purpose - Confirm ATC clearances to enter/cross an active runway in low visibility conditions
Configuration - Row of red, unidirectional, steady in pavement lights across the entire taxiway at the runway hold position, and elevated steady-burning red lights on either side
Following ATC clearance, the stop bar is turned off and the lead-on lights are turned on
Never cross a red illuminated stop bar even if you have received ATC clearance
If after crossing, the lead-on lights extinguish, hold position, and contact ATC for instruction
Runway Lighting
Runway End Identifier Lights (REIL)
Installed to provide rapid / positive identification of the approach end of a runway
Configuration - Pair of synchronized flashing lights on each side of the runway threshold
Runway Edge Light Systems (HIRL, MIRL, LIRL)
Outline the edges of runways during dark / restricted visibility conditions
Classified according to intensity/brightness: High Intensity (HIRL); Medium (MIRL); Low (LIRL)
Configuration
Runway edge lights - White
Instrument runways – Yellow for the last 2,000,’ or half the runway, whichever is shorter
Lights marking the end of the runway – Red / Green
Red indicates the end of the runway to a departing aircraft
Green indicates the threshold to landing aircraft
Runway Centerline Lighting System (RCLS)
Installed on some precision runways to facilitate landing under adverse conditions
Configuration
Along runway centerline at 50’ intervals
From the threshold, the lights are white until the last 3,000’ of the runway
White lights alternate with red for 2,000’, and the last 1,000’ all lights are red
Touchdown Zone Lights (TDZL)
On some precision runways to indicate touchdown zone in low visibility conditions
Configuration
Rows of (usually 3) lights on both sides of the runway centerline
Rows begin 100’ beyond the landing threshold and extend to 3,000’ beyond the landing threshold or the midpoint of the runway, whichever is less
Taxiway Centerline Lead-Off Lights
Provide visual guidance to exit the runway
Configuration
Alternate green & yellow lights, beginning with green, from the runway centerline to 1 light position beyond the runway hold position/ILS critical area hold position
Taxiway Centerline Lead-on Lights
Provide visual guidance for entering the runway
Configuration
Color coded with the same pattern as lead-off lights
Bidirectional (1 side emits light for the lead-on function the other for the lead-off)
Land and Hold Short Lights
Used to indicate the hold short point on certain runways approved for LAHSO
When installed, the lights will be on anytime LAHSO is in effect and off when not
Configuration - A row of pulsing white lights installed across the runway
Runway Status Lights (RWSL)
Fully automated system indicating that it’s unsafe to enter, cross, takeoff, or land on a runway
Installed at several major US airports
Processes information from surveillance systems to turn red warning lights on/off
Used in conjunction with ATC – lights and ATC instructions must agree
Runway Entrance Lights (REL)
In-pavement red lights
Warns aircraft waiting to cross/enter a runway that there’s conflicting traffic
Takeoff Hold Lights (THL)
In-pavement red lights
Warns aircraft in the takeoff position that the runway is occupied & takeoff is unsafe
More details: FAA Runway Status Lights
Control of Lighting Systems
Operation of approach light systems and runway lighting is controlled by the tower / FSS
Pilots may request the lights be turned on or off
Pilot Control of Airport Lighting
Radio control of lighting is available at some airports by keying the microphone
3 clicks for Low lights, 5 for Medium, and 7 for High
All clicks within 5 seconds – lasts 15 minutes
Frequency is in Chart Supplement/ instrument approach procedures publications (usually CTAF)
CE: Failure to comply with airport, runway, and taxiway lighting
Elements of Safe Taxi Operations  								AI.V.D.K1
The lesson as a whole discusses this topic
Conclusion: Brief review of the main points

paragraphs.text: V.F. Before Takeoff Check
Introduction
How
Before Takeoff Checklist
Engine Warm Up
Before takeoff check is usually performed after taxiing to a position near the runway/run-up area
Allows time to reach min temperatures ensuring lubrication and internal engine clearances
Positioning the Aircraft
A suitable location should be firm and free of debris (smooth, paved, or turf surface if possible)
There should not be anything behind the aircraft that might be damaged by the airflow
Point the airplane as closely as possible into the wind, and move forward slightly to straighten the nose
CE: Improper positioning of the airplane
RM: Division of Attention 									AI.V.F.R1
Attention must be divided inside and outside the aircraft
Excessive time with your head down (checklists, etc.) can result in unmonitored movement
Checklist 								AI.V.F.K1a. AI.V.F.K1b, AI.V.F.K1c
Prepares the aircraft for takeoff and checks critical flight equipment and systems
The before takeoff checklist provided by the manufacturer should be used to ensure a proper check
Never go solely off memory
Review the Before Takeoff Checklist with the learner
Discuss reasons for checking each item and how to detect errors
Go/No Go Decision
The PIC is responsible for determining whether the airplane is in a condition for safe flight
Use the criteria in the POH, as well as pilot judgement, to measure airplane performance
This is your chance to catch a problem while safely on the ground rather than in flight
If there is a problem, ask yourself, Are we still legal? Can the problem be fixed? Is this safe?
If there are any doubts, return to the ramp for further investigation
CE: Improper acceptance of marginal engine performance
RM: Departure Brief 										AI.V.F.R4
(RM: Potential engine failure or other malfunctions, considering operational factors)
Before takeoff, review the performance speeds, expected takeoff distance, & emergency procedures
VR, VX, VY - Announce the speeds
Takeoff on runway XX, we have X,XXX’ of runway, performance shows we need X,XXX’ today
In the case of an emergency:
Lose engine on roll, close the throttle, stop straight ahead, maintain control with rudder / brakes
Lose engine after rotation with runway available, land on the remaining runway
Lose engine above XXX’ AGL, attempt to turn back to the runway, otherwise land straight ahead
CE: Hazards of failure to review takeoff and emergency procedures
Don’t try to come up with a plan during an emergency
Before Entering the Runway
Visually check the area to ensure it is clear of anything that could be a hazard
Check the runway, as well as final approach
Remember, radio communication is not required at uncontrolled airports
RM: Consider Wake Turbulence 								AI.V.F.R3
Departing after a Large Aircraft
On the same runway: Rotate prior to their rotation point & climb above their path until turning clear
Executing a low approach, missed approach, or touch-and-go
Wait at least 2 minutes prior to a landing or takeoff
Vortex hazard may exist along the runway/in the flight path, particularly in a quartering tailwind
Intersection takeoffs on the same runway
Be alert to adjacent large aircraft operations, particularly upwind of the runway of intended use
Avoid headings that cross below the larger aircraft’s path
For more details, see lesson VI.B. Traffic Patterns - Wake Turbulence
Avoiding Incursions
Before moving, clear to the left, right and center
Monitor the appropriate frequency
Know where other aircraft are in relation to you
Repeat all clearances, and do not cross hold short lines without a clearance
If any doubt exists, stop, and wait for the traffic to clear
Clear final approach before taxiing into the takeoff position
CE: Failure to avoid incursions & ensure no conflict with traffic prior to taxiing into takeoff position
RM: Runway Change 										AI.V.F.R2
Don’t rush
Find a place to stop and make necessary changes
Performance
Adjust for changes in runway length, wind direction, runway gradient, terrain, procedures, etc.
Ensure adequate performance and safety
Update navigation equipment (GPS, VOR, etc.)
Departure Brief
Note differences and brief the departure for the new runway
Taxi Instructions
Review the taxi diagram
Request and readback taxi instructions
Confirm the route and begin the taxi
Conclusion:
Brief review of the main points

paragraphs.text: V.B. Flight Deck Management
References: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3), POH/AFM
Instructor Notes:
Introduction:
Attention
Interesting fact or attention-grabbing story
All pilots need to learn to be good housekeepers. The airplane is your house, and you need to be sure it stays clean and organized.
Overview
Review Objectives and Elements/Key ideas
What
Flight deck management (single pilot resource management) is a process that combines you, the airplane, and the environment for safer and more efficient operations.
Why
Understanding the elements behind flight deck management (single pilot resource management) provides for a considerably more efficient and safer flight.
How:
Passenger Briefing 											AI.V.B.K1
Safety Belts
FAR 91.107 - Each person must be briefed on how to fasten and unfasten their safety belt/shoulder harness
Cannot taxi, takeoff, land without ensuring each person has fastened their safety belt/shoulder harness
Briefing Topics
Combination of FAR 91.519 (Briefing requirements for Turbine-Powered Multiengine Airplanes and Fractional Aircraft), FAASafety Passenger Briefing and common topics
Identify the PIC
Safety belts and harnesses
Exits (how to operate the doors and emergency exits_
Additional pertinent emergency procedures
Fire extinguishers
Specific exit procedures, if necessary
Avoiding propeller blades
Gathering point in case of an evacuation
Passenger Conduct
Talking (i.e. sterile flight deck/not during taxi, takeoff, landing unless safety requires it)
See and avoid (pointing out other aircraft)
Location of survival equipment
Ditching procedures/flotation equipment
Systems
Use of oxygen systems (normal and/or emergency)
Heat/Air
No smoking
Questions
FAASafety passenger briefing discussion and briefing card – Passenger Briefing
Arranging & Securing 										AI.V.B.K4
Arranging
Ensure that all the necessary equipment, documents, checklists & navigation charts are on board
Materials should be neatly arranged and organized to make them readily available for use
Any equipment with wires should not interfere with the motion or operation of any controls
Securing
Secure all cargo to prevent movement during flight
Loose cargo could be hazardous to people and/or aircraft CG/balance
Check for loose articles which might be tossed about during flight, or in turbulence
Form the habit of “good housekeeping;” in the long run, it will pay off in safe and efficient flying
Seat Position & Controls
Seat Belt/Harnesses
When seated, the seat belt/harness should be adjusted to a comfortable, snug fit
Shoulder harness must be worn at least for taxi, takeoff, and landing
The safety belt must be worn all times at the controls
Seats
On each flight, the pilot should be seated in the same position
Adjust height for the proper viewing height as directed in the POH
The pilot(s) must be able to see inside and outside references
If the seat is adjustable, it is important to ensure that the seat is locked in position
Many accidents have occurred as the result of the seat suddenly moving with acceleration/deceleration
Rudder Pedals
Adjust the rudder pedals forward or backward
Knees should be slightly bent
With heels on the floor and balls of the feet on the pedals full movement should be available
Using toes, the brakes should be able to be actuated
Navigation Data Currency 										AI.V.B.K3
Charts
FAR 91.103 requires each PIC to become familiar with all available information concerning that flight
Although it doesn’t specifically require it, you should always carry current charts
Information changes rapidly, out of date charts may be missing crucial information
Ex: Changes to airspace, new special airspace, change to procedures, frequencies, etc.
To confirm currency, refer to the next scheduled edition date printed on the cover
Use the FAAs Dates of Latest Editions to verify you have the most current edition
Prior to expiration, check NOTAMs and Safety Alerts and Charting Notices for any changes
Database Currency
AIM 1-1-1b3(b): Databases must be maintained to the current update for IFR operations
No such requirements exist for VFR ops, however it is always a good idea to keep a current database
Violations
It is not FAA policy to initiate enforcement action against a pilot for having an old chart or no chart, or for having an expired navigation database

However, if a pilot is involved in an enforcement investigate and there is evidence that an out-of-date chart/database (or no chart) contributed to the situation, then that information could be used in any enforcement action that might be taken
Bottom line, use current charts/databases
Checklist Usage 											AI.V.B.K2
Ensure the proper and orderly use of the manufacturer’s checklist
Ensures every item is completed and checked in a logical order
Don’t go on memory, always backup your actions with a checklist
Sooner or later, you will make a mistake without a checklist
RM: Inoperative Equipment 									AI.V.B.R2
On the Ground
Perform a thorough preflight
Follow FAR 91.213(d) procedures to defer & placard equipment as inoperative
See III.B. Airworthiness Requirements
There should be no question as to what equipment is or isn’t operative
Consider the effects the inoperative equipment will have on the flight
Set and follow personal equipment minimums – just because it’s legal, doesn’t mean it’s safe
Ex: Inflight weather is not required by regs, but it could be hazardous without it on certain days
If you’re not comfortable with the state of the airplane, don’t fly it
Airborne
If equipment becomes inoperative, a decision must be made to continue or divert
Considerations
Would the equipment prevent flying if it happened on the ground? FAR 91.213(d)

paragraphs.text: V.C. Engine Starting

References: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3), Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25), Reduction of Electrical System Failures Following Aircraft Engine Starting (AC 91-55), Cold Weather Operation of Aircraft - Cancelled (AC 91-13), POH/AFM
Instructor Notes:
Introduction:
Attention
Interesting fact or attention-grabbing story

Starting the engine of an airplane is not as simple as starting the engine of your car. A plane can’t just be turned on anywhere at any time, the proper precautions and procedures must be followed for safety reasons.
Overview
Review Objectives and Elements/Key ideas
What
Engine Starting discusses the safety precautions necessary when starting an airplane, the different conditions which affect starting the engine, as well as different ways to start the engine.
Why

Proper engine starting is necessary for the safety of people and property, as well as to prevent engine damage. There are certain situations which require special procedures, and some procedures can be dangerous. It is very important to know the proper engine starting procedures and precautions.
How:
POH
Always use Manufacturer Checklists
Ensures every item is completed and checked in a logical order
Covers the Before Starting checklist and the Starting Engine Checklists
Especially important with different checklists for varying situations (Flooded, Cold, Normal, Hot, etc.)
Don’t go on memory, always backup your actions with a checklist
Sooner or later you will make a mistake without a checklist
RM: Engine Starting Limitations 								AI.V.C.K3, AI.V.C.R3
Check the Limitations section of the POH for applicable engine start limits
Starter limits, cooling limits between starts, etc.
RM: Safety Precautions (RM: Propeller Safety) 							AI.V.C.R1
Set the parking brake (ensuring they are pumped) and hold the brakes with your toes
Look outside to ensure you are not moving
Too much heads down time (checklists, checking indications, etc.) can result in unrecognized movement and an accident or damage to the aircraft
Ensure the ramp area surrounding the airplane is clear of persons, equipment, and other hazards
Be aware of what is in front of, and behind the airplane
Check all directions to ensure nothing is/will be in the vicinity of the propeller, or propeller blast
Propeller thrust can damage to property and injure people
Anti-collision lights should be turned on prior to any start, at night use position lights too
Always call “CLEAR” out of the side window and wait for a response from someone who may be nearby
When activating the starter, the wheel brakes must be depressed
Set the parking brake, if installed (and directed in the POH)
Proper brake application ensures the airplane does not lunge forward upon starting the engine
Keep one hand on the throttle for prompt response if RPM is excessive or a hazardous situation presents itself
Ensure the propeller area is clear of any obstructions (debris, people, obstacles, etc.)
Doublecheck the area behind the aircraft is clear
Engine Starting
Normal Start Checklist
Review the normal start checklist in the POH
Engine Controls During Start
Always keep one hand on the throttle to manage the initial engine starting speed
After the engine is started, set the throttle to the RPM setting specified in the POH
Other controls (mixture, prop, carb heat, boost pump, etc.) should be set/adjusted as specified in the POH/checklist
Monitor the oil pressure after engine start
Ensure the pressure is increasing toward the POH specified value
If normal oil pressure is not reached and maintained, serious internal engine damage is likely
In most conditions, oil pressure should reach at least the lower limit within 30 seconds
If oil pressure does not rise to the POH values in the specified time, shutdown the engine
Check all other instruments to ensure they are operating within limits
Avoid excessive engine RPM and temperatures
Adjust the engine controls to maintain the POH recommended RPM, fuel, propeller, etc. settings
Monitor the instruments and use the checklist if the engine temperature begins to rise abnormally
Atmospheric Conditions 									AI.V.C.K1
Cold Weather
Low temperatures may cause a change in the viscosity of engine oils (they congeal, or become thicker), batteries may lose a higher percentage of their effectiveness, and instruments may stick
Preheat of the engine(s) (and cabin) before starting is desirable
Preheat by storing the airplane in a heated hangar, if possible
Use only heaters that are in good condition and do not refuel the heater while it is operating
Do not leave the aircraft unattended and keep a fire extinguisher handy
Do not place the heat ducting so it will blow hot air directly on combustible parts of the aircraft (upholstery, canvas engine covers, flexible fuel, oil, and hydraulic lines)
Starting the Engine
In moderately cold weather, preheat may not be necessary
Use care, oil may be congealed and turning the engine with the starter or by hand is difficult
If approved by the POH, the pilot may rotate the prop by hand to loosen the congealed oil
Follow the POH procedures, and be positive the engine is OFF to avoid an accidental start
Cold Engine Start Problems
Tendency to overprime, which washes down cylinder walls and may result in scoring of the walls
Also results in poor compression and consequently causes hard starting
Aircraft fires have been started by overpriming
Have a fireguard/extinguisher ready
In a cold engine, icing over the sparkplug electrodes can cause problems
Engine only fires a few revolutions and then quits
Sufficient combustion to cause water in the cylinders, but not enough to heat them up
The water condenses on the sparkplug electrodes, freezes to ice, and shorts them out
Avoid prolonged idling
Engines may quit because sufficient heat is not produced to keep the plugs from fouling out
The only remedy is heat
If a heater is not available, the plugs should be removed from the engine and heated to the point where no moisture is present
Starting
Prime the engine with fuel first (over-priming can result in an aircraft fire – AC 91-13)
AC 91-13 is still available to read but has been cancelled and incorporated into various other ACs
After start, follow the POH procedures to allow the engine, and engine oil to warm and circulate
As mentioned, engines may quit with long idling
Hot Weather
Hot Start procedures in the POH
Generally, little to no priming is needed, but if the engine doesn’t catch, use minimum priming
In the case of an overprimed engine (common with hot starts), use the flooded start checklist to clear the excess fuel and start the engine
Vapor lock (fuel injected engines)
Fuel delivery lines tend to be on the top of the engine, directly over the cylinder fins
Heat from the engine/outside can boil the fuel out of the lines creating vapor & preventing start
Hot start attempts to purge/minimize the vapor in the system with the fuel boost pump
*Starting with External Power 								AI.V.C.K2, AI.V.C.R2
RM: Ensure proper use and understanding of the external power unit
Follow steps in the owner’s manual
Besides not being able to start the plane, there is the risk of damaging the unit or aircraft systems
In addition to those items in Section 4, Normal Operating Procedures, check the following items:
Caution Lights (EPU) - Illuminated if power is available
During preflight, check that the EPU connector is inserted and secure
Before Engine Starting
Engine Starting Checklist, plus:
EPU Light: ON; EPU Switch: ON; Voltmeter: Check 12 - 14 Volts
Start the engine as normal (Cold/Warm/Flooded)
After Engine Start
Select EPU switch to OFF: EPU light ON
Signal ground crew to pull the EPU cord: EPU light OFF
Master Switch (GEN): OFF and Check Battery Voltage: Approximately 12 volts
Master Switch (GEN) ON and Check Battery Voltage: Approximately 14 volts
GEN warning light: Check OFF
RM: Hand Propping Safety (RM: Propeller Safety) 							AI.V.C.R1
Basic requirements BEFORE attempting a hand prop
Do not hand prop unless two people, both familiar with hand propping techniques are available
Never allow a person unfamiliar with the controls to occupy the pilot’s seat when hand propping
The person pulling the propeller blades through directs all activity and is in charge of the procedure
Chocks can be an additional precaution, or tie down the tail (Be careful removing them)
The second person must be seated in the plane to ensure the brakes are set, the controls are properly exercised, and to follow the direction of the person pulling the propeller
The ground surface near the prop should be stable and free of debris (otherwise relocate)
Loose gravel, wet grass, mud, etc. might cause the person pulling the prop to slip into the blades
Both participants should discuss the procedure and agree on voice commands and expected action
*Engine Starting Set-up
The fuel system/engine controls (pump, primer, throttle, mixture) should be set for a normal start
Check to ensure the ignition/magneto switch is OFF
The descending prop blade should be rotated to a position slightly above horizontal
The person doing the propping should face blade squarely and stand less than an arm’s length away
Too far away and it would be necessary to lean forward in an unbalanced condition
*Procedures and Commands for Hand Propping
Person out front says, “GAS ON, SWITCH OFF, THROTTLE CLOSED, BRAKES SET”
Person IN ensures - Fuel: ON, Mixture: RICH, Ignition: OFF, Throttle: CLOSED, Brakes SET, and repeats
Person out front checks the brakes by pushing on the prop
Person out front, after pulling the prop through to prime the engine says, “BRAKES AND CONTACT”
Person in the pilot’s seat checks the brakes SET and turns the ignition switch ON, then repeats
The propeller is swung by forcing the blade downward rapidly as hard as possible
Push with the palms
If the blade is gripped tightly with the fingers, the person’s body may be drawn into the propeller blades should the engine misfire and rotate in the opposite direction
If it does not start, the prop should not be moved until certain the ignition/magneto switch is OFF
Conclusion:
Brief review of the main points
Always ensure safety when starting the engine.

Basic requirements BEFORE attempting a hand prop
Do not hand prop unless two people, both familiar with hand propping techniques are available
Never allow a person unfamiliar with the controls to occupy the pilot’s seat when hand propping
The person pulling the propeller blades through directs all activity and is in charge of the procedure
Chocks can be an additional precaution, or tie down the tail (Be careful removing them)
The second person must be seated in the plane to ensure the brakes are set, the controls are properly exercised, and to follow the direction of the person pulling the propeller
The ground surface near the prop should be stable and free of debris (otherwise relocate)
Loose gravel, wet grass, mud, etc. might cause the person pulling the prop to slip into the blades
Both participants should discuss the procedure and agree on voice commands and expected action
*Engine Starting Set-up
The fuel system/engine controls (pump, primer, throttle, mixture) should be set for a normal start
Check to ensure the ignition/magneto switch is OFF
The descending prop blade should be rotated to a position slightly above horizontal
The person doing the propping should face blade squarely and stand less than an arm’s length away
Too far away and it would be necessary to lean forward in an unbalanced condition

Person out front says, “GAS ON, SWITCH OFF, THROTTLE CLOSED, BRAKES SET”
Person IN ensures - Fuel: ON, Mixture: RICH, Ignition: OFF, Throttle: CLOSED, Brakes SET, and repeats
Person out front checks the brakes by pushing on the prop
Person out front, after pulling the prop through to prime the engine says, “BRAKES AND CONTACT”
Person in the pilot’s seat checks the brakes SET and turns the ignition switch ON, then repeats
The propeller is swung by forcing the blade downward rapidly as hard as possible
Push with the palms
If the blade is gripped tightly with the fingers, the person’s body may be drawn into the propeller blades should the engine misfire and rotate in the opposite direction
If it does not start, the prop should not be moved until certain the ignition/magneto switch is OFF

Brief review of the main points
